name: Ultra Red
lede: Ultra red is an obsolete name for infrared, so the pink swatch here shows only a screen stand-in, not the thing named.

sections.title: Beyond the red
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary records ultra red as an obsolete term for infrared [1]. Its entry for the prefix says *ultra*, as regards any particular colour, means on the deep side of that colour [1]. The prefix could therefore mean either more of a color or beyond it, which may be why the term faded [1].

The next entry shows the prefix at work. Ultramarine is a brilliant blue from lapis lazuli, used widely from the thirteenth century despite its high cost [1]. Its name means from overseas, since the main supply of lapis lazuli lay in Afghanistan, and Paterson credits Guimet with first synthesising it in 1828, in response to a prize of 6,000 francs, though other books record a rival claim [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is a bright pink with no historical standing as the thing named [2]. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, no work holds a color within six units of it across five per cent of the canvas [2]. Because infrared is not visible, no painting could show it directly [1].

origin.named_after: Latin ultra, beyond; later replaced by infrared
origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, p. 404

notes.cite: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, p. 404

questions.q: What does Paterson say ultra red is an obsolete term for?
Who first synthesised ultramarine in 1828, per Paterson?

openers: Ultra red is an old name for infrared, a kind of light we cannot see.

issues: Guimet 1828 attributed to Paterson, rival claim (Gmelin) noted
